questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: For me personally, it was crucial that the study destination i choose had English as a first language. Also, it was important for me that academically, I was not settling for something way less than what UCPH has to offer. That said, choosing a destination with a lot to offer besides the university part, was also important for me.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer:
Going on exchange is something you have to do yourself, meaning that it is your own responsibility to make sure you seek out all the important information. 
I know that McGill offers student buddies (much like the system at KU), also they provide emails, introdays, etc. so I didnt feel like i was missing important info.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: They inform you on almost everything via email. I also went to an introductory session with our contact person at McGill, used the "Ask McGill" shops around campus the first couple of days, so all in all it was a good experience.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer:
It would have been nice with some specific introductory events only for exchange students, but I didn't feel lost at all. 
Also know that KU generally has a pretty good deal with McGill, and so does some of the other Danish universities, meaning that there is a lot of Danes in Montreal around that time. Try to make contact with them beforehand, that way you are not alone when it comes to gathering all the necessary info.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Pretty easy - I found it beforehand with some fellow student from UCPH. 
Know that the student housing is nice because it allows you to meet a lot of other people, however it can be a bit expensive. 
I used a facebook group for McGill Off Campus Housing, there is a couple so it should be no problem. Be aware that some of the apartments are basement apartments with no windows, maybe that's not for everyone ;)
When it comes to choosing areas, being close to a metrostop is nice during the winter period. The McGill Ghetto and Plateau are two really nice areas.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Pick a place where the metro is close if it is not too close to campus, this will come in handy during winter times.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer:
The student housing offered is pretty expensive compared to what you pay off-campus, just have that in mind. 
Generally, there is plenty of housing in Montreal, so when it comes to distance to campus, and the lenght of the lease, its fair to be picky.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had no problems with the registration at McGill, I have even emailed with the student service when I was in doubt, also with no problems.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
The system is rather easy, but you have to be fast. 
Once the course registration opens, a lot of the smaller courses are quickly filled up, so you might find yourself lacking the course you wanted. I had picked out 4 courses and only ended up getting two, luckily I had a plan A, B and C where i knew there would be no scheduling conflicts. 
Also know that you are only required by UCPH to take 4 courses, but you can sign up for 5. I signed up for 5, then during the add-drop period I just had to drop one, but I had a hance to go see what the course was about and meet the profs. 
Also know that during the add-drop period you have a pretty good chance of getting into a course that was initially filled, you just have to check the registration page a few times a day.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Student Service at McGill are really helpful :)

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Well, I only got 2/4 of the courses I initially wanted, but the two other I got instead where just as good (one i even think might have been a better option than my originally plan)

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Register for 5 courses, so you have one to spare if you find out during your Add-drop period that the course wasn't what you expected (The course descriptions at McGill ae pretty sparse). 
Be aware of your schedule, if you are smart you can give yourself a short week, which is really nice for longer trips during your exchange. 
Be aware of the type of course load and exams you are signing up for. I ended up with 4 in person exams in a week, which i not recommendable ;)
If you can, choose at least one course where the exam is not in person, but also be aware of not ending up with 4 courses that all have weekly assignments. In total, be smart.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: McGill does not offer their lab courses to exchange students. Other than that I think the academic level just really depends on the courses you choose.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The level of the course kinda responds to the year you are in, meaning that level 100 courses are for first year students, 200 for second year etc. With that being said, as a bachelors student from UCPH it is manageable to have a few of your courses being level 400-500 courses, just be aware that you might need a confirmation from the prof before choosing said course. 
Also, don't be shy to choose a 100-200 level course if the subject is completely new to you, as the introductory courses are usually 100-200.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: I only had lecture style courses, where the lectures were very much like the ones at UCPH, but without the TØ sessions, so you are a bit more on your own. A lot of the other Danes had smaller class like courses where it was more discussion based, and they seemed to enjoy it - so I guess it just depend on the course you take.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
PHAR300 - Drug Action
MIMM324 - Fundamental Virology
COMP204 - Programming For Life Science
PSYC311 - Human Cognition and the Brain

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
COMP204 is a really nice programming course, very basic and manageable. It has weekly assignments and quizzes that count for a part of your grade, which can be a bit overwhelming during the course, but this also means that if you do well in the weekly assignments, you can pass the course whit out attending the exam. 
MIMM324 is also a really nice course, some of the profs are not the best, but the general structure of the course, and the topics are really interesting. During the course, there are quizzes and two assignments, but they are pretty manageable. 
PSYC311 is also a really nice course when it comes to the lectures and topics, there is a bit of work in getting to know all the neuroanatomy needed (it is not a lot, but still), but I was really glad i took it. 
PHAR300 is the only one of my courses that I can't really recommend. It seemed fine in the beginning, and some of the topics are really interesting, but the detail level of the midterm/exam is just a lot compared to what is touched during the lectures, and to top it of, no lecture slides are handed out. That being said, some of the topics were nice, it was just not what I expected.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I think i budgettet very conservatory before i left, so there wasn't really anything that took me by suprise.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Some supermarket items are more expensive than in Denmark, some are less. Also the tax+tip when you are out can really be confusing in the beginning

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: McGill has a lot of clubs, so there is something for everyone.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just about every club imaginable, from sports to chocolate clubs.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
Frosh is really fun, but consider whether you are more a outdoor or faculty frosh kind of type. 
Also, join a club or sports so you can meet other people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Toronto is relatively close, also there is a thing calles MustBus that arrange busses to a number of different destinations during the semester for cheap prices. Also, all the major car rental services has (Enterprise, Avis and Hertz), so you can get cheaper rentals.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Pretty easy - Montreal has a almost europe-vibe. However, I was a bit surprised at how much French is spoken, it truly is the first language in Montreal.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: JOIN THE CLUBS!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer:
The amount of French spoken in Montreal can be a bit challenging, eg. when you are in a metro that stops running and they only give announcements in French, but you get over it pretty fast. 
Another thing is the age of the local students, they are generally a bit younger than we are because they start uni at a younger age.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Montreal is just a really nice city to live in. It is a big city, with high rise buildings and busy streets, but it is also a city that is relatively old for north American standards, and has a lot of cultural things going on.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Pay attention when choosing your courses.
Make sure to spend some time outside Montreal, rent a car, go on hikes, have fun. 
Make as much use of the summer that is left for you, once it gets colder it is no fun experiencing the city.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: McGill is a large university, so it can be a bit overwhelming in the beginning, but you get used to the vibe pretty fast.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: For me, it was just doing something fun and different for a semester, and also having to prioritise my time a bit different in order to both experience Montreal/Canada while I was there, as well as attending university at the same time.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To get to meet the locals. McGill has a lot of exchange students, and a lot of the fultime students are also not from the local area, but other exchange students can be just as nice :)

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
